pos: n. (a magical figure supposed to draw heavenly influence)
etymology: Webster (1828) enters TAL’ISMAN without an etymology note; this entry does not supply one.
biblical_def: A talisman is an object made under astrological rites and believed to carry power. Webster (1828) defines it as “a magical figure cut or engraved under certain superstitious observances of the configuration of the heavens, to which wonderful effects are ascribed,” or “the seal, figure, character or image of a heavenly sign, constellation or planet, engraven on a sympathetic stone, or on a metal corresponding to the star, in order to receive its influence.” He records that such things “were held to be preservatives against all kinds of evils.” A talisman joins two things Scripture forbids: trust in an object and the worship of the heavens. God mocked Babylon’s “astrologers, the stargazers, the monthly prognosticators”, who could not “save thee from these things that shall come upon thee” (Isa 47:13). Israel was told, “Learn not the way of the heathen, and be not dismayed at the signs of heaven” (Jer 10:2). At Ephesus, believers “which used curious arts brought their books together, and burned them before all men” (Act 19:19).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): TALISMAN, a magical figure engraved under superstitious observance of the heavens, to receive the influence of a star; held to preserve against evils.
webster_full: TAL'ISMAN, noun

1. A magical figure cut or engraved under certain superstitious observances of the configuration of the heavens, to which wonderful effects are ascribed; or it is the seal, figure, character or image of a heavenly sign, constellation or planet, engraven on a sympathetic stone, or on a metal corresponding to the star, in order to receive its influence. The talismans of the Samothracians were pieces of iron, formed into images and set in rings, etc. They were held to be preservatives against all kinds of evils.
Talismans are of three kinds, astronomical, magical and mixed. Hence,
2. Something that produces extraordinary effects; as a talisman to destroy diseases.
corruption_summary: Talisman is now used loosely for any lucky object or mascot, and its root in astrology is forgotten.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s talisman was astrological: an image made to receive the influence of a planet or star. Modern speech uses the word for a lucky charm, a mascot, or anything that seems to bring success, and the claim behind it goes unexamined.

Webster’s second sense, “something that produces extraordinary effects,” shows how easily the language of magic passes into ordinary praise. Scripture’s answer is the same as for the amulet: such things are given up (Act 19:19), because power belongs to God.
roots_summary: A figure engraved under the stars to receive their influence: magic joined to astrology.

etymology: Greek neos, new, and phyton, a plant: one newly planted. Webster (1828) enters NEOPHYTE without an etymology note.
biblical_def: A neophyte is one newly come to the faith. Webster (1828) gives three senses: “a new convert or proselyte; a name given by the early Christians to such heathens as had recently embraced the Christian faith”; “a novice; one newly admitted to the order of priest”; and “a tyro; a beginner in learning.” He adds that such converts “were considered as regenerated by baptism,” which records the early church’s belief, not Scripture’s teaching. The New Testament speaks tenderly of the new believer: “As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby” (1Pe 2:2). Paul spoke to the Corinthians “as unto babes in Christ” (1Co 3:1). It also warns against setting a new convert over the church. A bishop must be “Not a novice, lest being lifted up with pride he fall into the condemnation of the devil” (1Ti 3:6).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): NEOPHYTE, a new convert or proselyte, the early Christians’ name for recent converts from heathenism; a novice; a beginner.
webster_full: NEOPHYTE, noun
1. A new convert or proselyte; a name given by the early Christians to such heathens as had recently embraced the Christian faith, and were considered as regenerated by baptism.
2. A novice; one newly admitted to the order of priest.
3. A tyro; a beginner in learning.
corruption_summary: Neophyte now means any beginner in any field, and its Christian origin as a name for new converts is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s first sense is ecclesiastical: the early church’s name for heathens newly converted. Today a neophyte is any beginner, at a trade, a sport or a hobby. The word has lost the picture of a soul newly planted in Christ.

Webster also records that such converts “were considered as regenerated by baptism.” That is a report of early belief, not a rule of Scripture. The new birth is the work of the Spirit through the word (1Pe 2:2), and baptism signifies it but does not cause it.

pos: n. (a ruler; a clergyman in charge of a parish)
etymology: Latin rector, a ruler. Webster (1828): “Latin rector from rego, rectum, to rule.”
biblical_def: A rector is literally a ruler. Webster (1828) gives that sense first, “a ruler or governor,” with the example “God is the supreme rector of the world,” and notes “this application of the word is unusual.” In church use a rector is “a clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish, and has the tithes, etc.” Webster also gives the head of certain universities and schools, and “the superior officer or chief of a convent or religious house.” Scripture recognizes rule in the church, but always as service under Christ. “Let the elders that rule well be counted worthy of double honour, especially they who labour in the word and doctrine” (1Ti 5:17). A bishop rules “as the steward of God” (Tit 1:7), and those who rule “watch for your souls, as they that must give account” (Heb 13:17). Over all of them stands one Master: “one is your Master, even Christ; and all ye are brethren” (Mat 23:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): RECTOR, a ruler or governor; a clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish; the head of some universities or religious houses.
webster_full: REC'TOR, noun [Latin rector from rego, rectum, to rule.]
1. A ruler or governor.
God is the supreme rector of the world.
[This application of the word is unusual.]
2. A clergyman who has the charge and cure of a parish, and has the tithes, etc.; or the parson of an unimpropriated parish.

3. The chief elective officer of some universities, as in France and Scotland. The same title was formerly given to the president of a college in New England, but it is now in disuse. In Scotland, it is still the title of the head master of a principal school.
4. The superior officer or chief of a convent or religious house; and among the Jesuits, the superior of a house that is a seminary or college.
corruption_summary: Rector is now only a title of rank, and its plain meaning, ruler, with the duty of care that went with the cure of a parish, is no longer heard.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster kept the root meaning in view: a rector is a ruler, from Latin rego. In church use the word came to mean the holder of a parish living, and now it is only a title. The weight of “the charge and cure of a parish”, the care of souls, slips out of sight.
Scripture never lets church rule become ownership. Elders rule as stewards (Tit 1:7) who must give account (Heb 13:17), and all are brethren under one Master (Mat 23:8).

pos: n. (an ecclesiastical dignitary below a bishop)
etymology: Greek archi-, chief, and deacon. Webster (1828) refers the reader to DEACON.
biblical_def: An archdeacon is a chief officer under a bishop in a diocese. Webster (1828) defines him as, “In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary, next in rank below a bishop, who has jurisdiction either over a part or over the whole diocese.” He is “usually appointed by the bishop,” and “has a court, the most inferior of ecclesiastical courts, for hearing ecclesiastical causes, and the punishment of offenders by spiritual censures.” The office is a later development; Scripture’s deacons serve tables, not courts. The first deacons were chosen as “men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, whom we may appoint over this business” (Act 6:3), so that the apostles could give themselves “continually to prayer, and to the ministry of the word” (Act 6:4). Deacons must be “grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre” (1Ti 3:8). Christ’s rule for greatness applies to every rank: “whosoever will be great among you, let him be your minister” (Mat 20:26).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ARCHDEACON, in England an ecclesiastical dignitary next below a bishop, with jurisdiction over part or all of a diocese and a court of his own.
webster_full: ARCHDE'ACON, noun [See Deacon.]

In England, an ecclesiastical dignitary, next in rank below a bishop, who has jurisdiction either over a part or over the whole diocese. He is usually appointed by the bishop, and has an authority originally derived from the bishop, but now independent of him. He has a court, the most inferior of ecclesiastical courts, for hearing ecclesiastical causes, and the punishment of offenders by spiritual censures.
corruption_summary: The archdeacon is a ranking church judge and administrator, an office far removed from the serving deacon of Acts 6, though the name joins them.
corruption_paragraphs: The word keeps the name deacon, a servant, but Webster describes a dignitary with jurisdiction and a court. The New Testament deacon was appointed so the apostles could keep to prayer and the word (Act 6:4); the archdeacon became an officer of discipline and administration.
The point is not that order and oversight are wrong, but that titles can carry a meaning the office has lost. Christ’s word stands over every rank: the great must be the minister (Mat 20:26).

pos: n. (a meeting of dissenters for worship)
etymology: Latin conventiculum, a small assembly, from conventus, a meeting. Webster (1828) gives only “Latin.”
biblical_def: A conventicle is an assembly for worship outside the established church. Webster (1828) defines it as “an assembly or meeting; usually applied to a meeting of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship,” noting that “in this sense it is used by English writers and in English statutes. Hence, an assembly, in contempt.” He adds that “in the United States, this word has no appropriate application.” His second sense is “a secret assembly or cabal; a meeting for plots.” English law once punished such meetings. The church of the apostles met in houses: at Mary’s house “many were gathered together praying” (Act 12:12), and Paul greeted “the church that is in their house” (Rom 16:5). When forbidden to preach, the apostles answered, “We ought to obey God rather than men” (Act 5:29). God hears His people when they meet: “Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it” (Mal 3:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): CONVENTICLE, an assembly, usually a meeting of dissenters from the established church for worship; hence an assembly in contempt; a secret cabal.
webster_full: CONVENTICLE, noun [Latin]

1. An assembly or meeting; usually applied to a meeting of dissenters from the established church, for religious worship. In this sense it is used by English writers and in English statutes. Hence, an assembly, in contempt. In the United States, this word has no appropriate application, and is Little Used, or not at all.
2. A secret assembly or cabal; a meeting for plots.
corruption_summary: The word was a term of contempt for lawful worship by dissenters, and it lumped godly assemblies together with plots.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster records that conventicle came to mean “an assembly, in contempt.” English statutes used it to forbid worship outside the established church, and the same word meant a cabal or a meeting for plots. A gathering for prayer was named as if it were a conspiracy.

Webster also notes that in the United States the word had no proper use, since there was no established church to dissent from. Scripture does not make the lawfulness of worship depend on a state license; the church met in houses (Rom 16:5) and obeyed God rather than men (Act 5:29).

etymology: English free and thinker. Webster (1828) enters FREE’THINKER without an etymology note.
biblical_def: A freethinker is one who rejects revealed religion. Webster (1828) defines the word bluntly: “A softer name for a deist; an unbeliever; one who discards revelation.” The name claims that the mind is free only when it has thrown off God’s word. Scripture describes the result differently: “Professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom 1:22). Peter foresaw “scoffers, walking after their own lusts” (2Pe 3:3), and Jude “mockers in the last time, who should walk after their own ungodly lusts” (Jud 1:18). The thinking that rejects revelation is not free but bound. Christ said, “If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed” (Joh 8:36), and “ye shall know the truth, and the truth shall make you free” (Joh 8:32).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FREETHINKER, a softer name for a deist; an unbeliever; one who discards revelation.
webster_full: FREE'THINKER, noun A softer name for a deist; an unbeliever; one who discards revelation.
corruption_summary: Freethinker presents unbelief as independence of mind, a softer name, as Webster said, for the rejection of revelation.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster saw through the word: it is “a softer name for a deist.” Those who rejected revelation chose a title that made faith look like bondage and unbelief look like freedom. The label still works that way when skeptics call themselves free thinkers.

Scripture reverses the claim. Those who professed wisdom apart from God “became fools” (Rom 1:22), and true freedom comes by the truth and by the Son (Joh 8:32, 36). A mind that will not receive God’s word is not free of authority; it has only put itself in God’s place.

pos: n. and adj. (one wild in religious opinion)
etymology: Latin fanaticus, belonging to a temple, inspired, from fanum, a temple. Webster (1828): “Latin fanaticus, phanaticus.”
biblical_def: A fanatic is one carried beyond reason in religion. Webster (1828) defines the adjective as “wild and extravagant in opinions, particularly in religious opinions; excessively enthusiastic; possessed by a kind of frenzy,” and the noun as “a person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects.” He adds that “fanatics sometimes affect to be inspired or to have intercourse with superior beings.” Scripture commends zeal but not frenzy. Paul bore Israel record “that they have a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2), and confessed his own former zeal: “Concerning zeal, persecuting the church” (Php 3:6). True zeal is “fervent in spirit; serving the Lord” (Rom 12:11), and worship is ordered: “For God is not the author of confusion, but of peace” (1Co 14:33); “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). Against claims of private inspiration stands the test: “believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God” (1Jn 4:1).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FANATIC, wild and extravagant in religious opinions; excessively enthusiastic; one who indulges wild notions of religion and sometimes affects inspiration.
webster_full: FANAT'IC,
FANAT'ICAL, adjective [Latin fanaticus, phanaticus.]
Wild and extravagant in opinions, particularly in religious opinions; excessively enthusiastic; possessed by a kind of frenzy. Hence we say, fanatic zeal; fanatic notions or opinions.
FANAT'IC,

FANAT'ICAL, noun A person affected by excessive enthusiasm, particularly on religious subjects; one who indulges wild and extravagant notions of religion, and sometimes exhibits strange motions and postures, and vehement vociferation in religious worship. Fanatics sometimes affect to be inspired or to have intercourse with superior beings.
corruption_summary: Fanatic is now thrown at any believer who takes Scripture seriously, so that ordinary conviction is treated as frenzy.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster’s fanatic is marked by “wild and extravagant” notions, frenzy, and claims of special inspiration. Today the word is often aimed at anyone who holds firm religious convictions, as if certainty itself were madness. Festus said the same of Paul: “much learning doth make thee mad” (Act 26:24).

The opposite error is to excuse real fanaticism as zeal. Scripture distinguishes the two: zeal must be “according to knowledge” (Rom 10:2), worship must be decent and orderly (1Co 14:40), and every claimed spirit must be tried (1Jn 4:1).

pos: n. (holiness, or the appearance of it)
biblical_def: Sanctimony once meant holiness itself. Webster (1828) defines it as “holiness; devoutness; scrupulous austerity; sanctity, or the appearance of it,” and marks it “Little Used.” The phrase “or the appearance of it” is where the word turned. Scripture warns against holiness that is only shown. Christ said the hypocrites “love to pray standing in the synagogues and in the corners of the streets, that they may be seen of men” (Mat 6:5), and “all their works they do for to be seen of men” (Mat 23:5). They were “like unto whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men’s bones” (Mat 23:27). Paul warned of those “Having a form of godliness, but denying the power thereof” (2Ti 3:5), and of rules that have “a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SANCTIMONY, holiness; devoutness; scrupulous austerity; sanctity, or the appearance of it. Little used.
webster_full: SANC'TIMONY, noun [Latin sanctimonia.] Holiness; devoutness; scrupulous austerity; sanctity, or the appearance of it. [Little Used.]
corruption_summary: Sanctimony now means only a false show of holiness, so that the word for holiness has become a word for hypocrisy.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster gave both meanings: “sanctity, or the appearance of it.” Modern usage has kept only the second, and sanctimonious means self-righteous. The drift shows how often the world has seen piety put on for display.

The danger is that every sign of devotion gets dismissed as sanctimony. Scripture condemns the show, not the substance: prayer “that they may be seen of men” (Mat 6:5), not prayer; a form of godliness without its power (2Ti 3:5), not godliness.
